utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. As indicated already yesterday, the Chamber is sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence in the absence of Judge Mindua. Welcome to you again, Mr. Sladojevic. The witness should be brought in, please. We are going into closed session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wish peace unto this house, and to all the present. I wish that the present court day end in keeping with God's will, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I greet Mr. Savcic and wish him a pleasant stay among us in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask e-court to display 07393 to see where we left off yesterday and to ask a couple of more questions on the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters cannot hear very well. It seems that an extra microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We discussed RPG training mines yesterday, and we were on page 27 of this rule. This is page 27.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask that it be displayed in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We discussed this RPG shell as used in combat against infiltrated groups. I'm reading 37 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, one request of the interpreters. Could you please move the microphone a little bit towards you. Thank you very much. One question: Is there an English translation available? Not yet. Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We are reading from paragraph 37 of the rule on RPG chemical training mines. The paragraph is called "Utilisation." "37. RPG chemical training mines or shells, in view of their purpose, may be very successfully used in peacetime against infiltrated groups and suppressing riots, resistance, and insurgence in war in all types of combat operations. The requirements for use are in keeping with the provisions of points 23 through 28 of this rule." You said that you used these RPGs to prevent desertion. Can they be used in peacetime and in war, in all types of combat operations, these RPGs, chemical training RPGs, can they be used in peacetime and in war, in all types of combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may be used both in war and in peacetime. In war, they may be used in all types of combat operations and, if necessary, I can share with you my personal experience of the use of these chemical training RPGs in war and their shortcomings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: There will perhaps be time for that. Tell us what you know about it.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My experience of using these RPGs in combat operations is rather negative, and the main reason for this is the fact that these are rifle grenades whose successful range, if I'm not mistaken, is 100 to 150 metres. Now the problem is this: The problem is, if I want to use this asset against an armed enemy, he has fire-power that is at least 400 metres in range, so if I want to use this asset against an armed enemy, I am bringing myself and my men into a disadvantageous tactical position. That is my experience, and it is negative. So from my point of view, my experience in using this asset in combat operations is very negative, and, as a commanding officer, I would really never use it. Unless perhaps in ideal circumstances such as an ideal tactical position, then perhaps I could use it, because using it in open air is practically pointless because this small quantity of this chemical used mainly by the police disperses very quickly in open air and has no effect against enemy manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you say, for the record, so that it's clear to all of us, does the person using this chemical have to approach the enemy not less than 150 metres, in order for this chemical RPG to have any effect?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I was trying to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us look at item 40 of the same rule. That's on the next page. We see it says how to use it in encirclement and blockade. "Encircling and blocking an enemy group follows detection for the purpose of capture or destruction such action is to be conducted with an increased number of grenades. Bearing in mind the direction of the wind, there is a higher risk of contaminating one's own personnel. The use of these grenades must be harmonised with strong fire and movement. These grenades are used in a larger quantity on the terrain targeted by the wind. In the event of extremely bad wind, it is -- it makes more sense to use chemical training RPGs by directly inserting them into space or into an opening in the facility where the group is located." Is this the reason why it's difficult to use this type of RPG in open terrain?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All these are aggravating circumstances, and I would like to draw your attention to one more factor. Since the personnel in the Army of Republika Srpska was mainly armed with automatic rifles, M70 -- there were several models but the basic model was M70. This type of weapon, unlike the previous generation which was the semi-automatic rifle, did not have an in-built RPG. To use this grenade, you had to put into the mouth of the barrel this RPG accessory. If you do that, you disable the basic purpose of weapon. You can use it then only for firing RPGs. To fire RPGs, you use special ammunition, that is, ammunition without rounds, without ammunition. So you practically disarm yourself for other types of combat. You cannot respond to infantry fire that would be directed at you. So all of these are negative factors against using this type of asset, and I always thought it was rather a marketing success then a really good combat asset.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we draw a brief conclusion? If a soldier would be using this grenade, would he be exposing himself to the enemy because he cannot defend himself from the weapon from which he fires this non-lethal grenade?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment when you apply the RPG accessory to the barrel, you can use the rifle only to fire RPGs, be it a chemical RPG or any other RPGs. He cannot -- or, rather, you cannot use that weapon for its basic purpose as an infantry weapon, and unless you have a very good cover, you become an easy target, a sitting duck before an armed enemy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now scroll down this page, 29. I meant scroll up. We see here in 41, "operating from ambush," "firing from ambush." It's my mistake. We want actually paragraph 42. We can see that it can be used in encirclement and blockade, from ambush. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It can also be used in controlling riots, resistance and insurgence. "42, chemical training RPGs maybe use are for controlling mass riots, protests and other riots, resistance and insurgency that may be threatening the safety of people, socially owned and private property on a larger scale, and the security of the country." My question is: In peacetime, was it allowed to use this asset, this agent, in suppressing riots?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But if this is used by military police units, certain pre-conditions had to be met. Namely, to proclaim a state of emergency on the whole territory, or part of the territory, and then following a decision by the Presidency of Yugoslavia, as it was then, it would be used by army units for controlling large-scale riots, such as those we had beginning with 1981 until the beginning of the conflict and that's a time when the army was used in part of our territory, and these units used these chemical training RPGs. So they with used in peacetime and in war, and in some corners of the world, they are being used on a daily basis when the authorities decide it is necessary to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender 07393. We have just shown in e-court what the witness was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to ask you if you could repeat the title of this document because you didn't mention it today, and it is it not listed in the documents to be used during cross-examination. I didn't find it. Perhaps there is -- you have used another number; I have no idea. I didn't find it. Please read into the record the title of this document so that we know what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. These are the rules for M83 rifle grenades. We have discussed the manner of use and application of this chemical agent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 07393.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I saw you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was, Mr. President. And that was just to point out to the Court that we do find that document on the list of exhibits that the Defence filed. Perhaps it was an updated one we received but the Court didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I looked through it but I didn't find it. Nevertheless, Mr. Tolimir, you have used some paragraphs, not because there is any concern about tendering this document, I'm sometimes a bit concerned about the amount of work for the translation unit. Do you really need all 40 pages translated into English? Therefore, it is perhaps possible that you just tender those pages you have used with the witness. Would that be convenient for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has tendered this document to show that Tolimir was involved in a criminal activity, as well as all the others who used this training asset. I would think that it would be useful to translate the entire document. However, if you are of the opinion that we should tender it -- only some of the parts of these rules, then we will send you a submission to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, can you help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I can, Mr. President. I think I can anyway. I don't believe that we have tendered this document. I'm not sure that we have used it as yet. I think we might have. But I don't believe it has been tendered by the Prosecution. If there are specific -- specific provisions -- and I think generally General Tolimir has been dealing with non-lethal chemical assets, such as CS gas and maybe BZ, I'm not sure, but I think there are specific provisions in this manual that deal with those types of chemical assets which I think he can identify. Because it is a rather large volume, it should be relatively simple to identify those relevant sections and have them translated. But we don't object if he would rather tender the entire -- the entire manual and have that translated. But I do agree with the Court that it would seem to be a lot of work for the translation people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. First, you are right. It is in the list; I didn't find it. So small, and there are so many documents. That is point five. The other is it is up to you. If you are tendering the whole document, we will ask the translation unit to translate the whole document; but if you consider it sufficient to have just your relevant parts, it would be helpful for the translation unit. What is your position, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be grateful to you. Since Mr. McCloskey was the first one to use this document in examining a witness, I believe that it would be beneficial for the Trial Chamber to have all of it translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. The whole document will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7393 shall be assigned Exhibit D290, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to call up P01297, which later became D202.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: These are the rules of engagement of military police in the armed forces of the SFRY. While we're waiting for the document to appear, I would like to ask you whether the rules of the former JNA were used in the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that we used all the rules of the former JNA. However, those rules were marked as having been adopted, which meant that they had a limited period of duration, until new rules were adopted by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see Article 36 of the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's see what you have just told us about who is it who is authorised to approve the use of those agents. Let's look at Article 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I was told that the P number is correct, P1297; but the document, D202, seems to be a different document. Just for the record. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We have Article 36 in front of us. And it reads, and I quote: "The military police may use other means of coercion, chemical means for temporary incapacitation, special vehicles, devices for forcibly halting vehicles only in emergencies, if their use is authorised by a commander of the army or another high-ranking military officer." Please, in our case did the Main Staff have the right to approve the use of those agents? Did officers in the Main Staff have the right to use them since they were at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Main Staff was at the level of command which had the right to approve the use of coercion means listed in Article 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have much time and you have answered my question. We are not going to look at all the possibilities provided by the rules of service. Let us now look at another document, which arrived at the command of the Drina Corps from the Main Staff and which deals with the use of means of coercion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up P2155. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This telegram was sent by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska by the sector for logistics, the technical department. It was sent on the 21st of July, 1995, to the command of the 27th Logistics Base, the command of the Drina Corps and the command of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. Under 1, it says: "The command of the 27th Logistics Base for the needs of" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Bullet point 1 says: "The command of the 27th Logistics Base shall transport the following items to the Drina Corps. Under 1, chemical rifle grenade, SDK M83, 50; chemical rifle grenade SKE M83, 58 pieces; and number 3, special hand-grenades, M79, AG-1, 40 pieces" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you should give a hard copy to the witness. It is nearly illegible on the screen. Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Do you know what kind of agents are in question here? Are they training agents or combat agents, or assets?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what these are. One of those assets we have just seen mentioned in the rules dealing with that asset. The second asset under 2 is a similar asset. It is also a rifle -- chemical training RPG. I don't know whether this is 83?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, it is 83.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, it is the same model. I don't know why it is repeated twice. And, finally, special hand-grenades AG-1, 40 pieces, this is a hand-grenade. Its range or its manner of use is the following: A soldier has to throw it by hand at a distance, an average distance of 30 to 40 metres. The charge is the same as for the rifle grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Please, here in the telegram it says - let me not read it - that the assets were sent from the base to one of your battalions, and that that battalion of yours will dispatch the assets to the Drina Corps. There were questions heard here as to how come that the battalion of the military police had to secure those assets. Tell me, if those assets could only be used by the military police pursuant to an order by an authorised officer, is it then necessary for the military police to secure the transport, the assets, to those to whom they are intended? And the second question: In wartime, all the transports that were sent to the Drina Corps through the combat areas, did they have to be secure by the military policemen whose area of authority that was? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The transport of ammunition and mines falls under the so-called special transports. As a rule, such transports are secured by the military police, or members of either state or public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you've told us that we have already seen, under 1 and 2, a reference to the chemical training RPG, SKD M83 and SKE M83, which are similar. Let's look at number 3, special hand-grenade, M79, AG-I. I would like to call up P2225. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P225. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record this is Exhibit P2225. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can see that these are the rules to use special hand-grenades, M79. Can we now look at page 3. Page 4. Thank you. In the English, it's page 4. Thank you. Please go back to the previous page in Serbian. Thank you. Here we can see bullet point 4. I'm going to quote: "Special hand grenades BRS M79 AG -- 2, figure 3 is a pyrotechnical chemical hand-grenade filled with tear-gas, CS. The tear-gas enters the atmosphere by means of combustion of the pyrotechnical mixture and evaporation followed by sudden cooling ..." Can we go to the following page in Serbian, please. "... that sublimates the vapour into solid particles that form toxic smoke in the air."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, is this the special hand-grenade, M79 A? We just saw a document accompanying the delivery of those weapons to the Drina Corps, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the special hand-grenade, M79, AG-1. This is not very legible. Could we go to the previous document that His Honour, the Presiding Judge, provided on paper, to explain these acronyms. Under 1, a smoke chemical training RPG, M83, 50 pieces. Under 2, explosive chemical training RPG, M83, 58 pieces. The difference between these two is the following. The grenade under number 2 has no CS in its composition. Instead, it has a very limited amount of explosive. I did troop testing with this to make sure, if we ever use this grenade in a real situation, you would have to hang the grenade on something, on a hook. You would have to ignite it. And in the immediate vicinity, you would have to stretch nylon, and then you test it by seeing whether it penetrates the nylon sheet at 50 metres. It causes a strong detonation but does not inflict injury. In peacetime, that's okay. So it's used to cause slight concussion and confuse. In war, after much stronger explosions, it looks like a shot from a rifle after a cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now look at this M79 AG-1, special hand-grenade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page. That's not the one we had -- that's it. It says "Special hand-grenade, BRS M79, AG-1," as written in the document in which these assets were sent to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know the range of this grenade? At how many metres did you have to approach the enemy to use it in war?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even in peace, under ideal circumstances, that means when you don't have to worry that the life of the person using it could be in jeopardy, the average range of throwing is 30, 40 metres. It is thrown by hand by pulling this security lock and then throwing it. I personally never had such ideal circumstances in combat. That would mean that I would have to approach an armed enemy at 30 metres in order to throw it. It's hard to imagine ever having such circumstances. So it's very problematic to use these special or regular hand-grenades without exposing your own personnel to fire.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at page 12 of this same instruction. It's just before this page. Or after this page. Page 12. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We'll lose a lot of time on this, but do you see this picture? Do you see the person throwing the grenade had to practically come up to the open window, in open air, in order to throw it into the room? That's page 13 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please zoom in on the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's perfectly clear. This is one of the examples how this can be used under the rules, but tactical and combat situations are something entirely different. So this is practically pure theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In situations of danger, would it be more dangerous to use this type of asset for the person using it than for the person being targeted by it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The consequences for the person targeted by this asset, by this grenade, would be problems with the eyes, teary eyes, itching around the eyes that impairs vision. That's the only consequence of being targeted; whereas being targeted by fire, everybody knows, it only depends on the degree of injury and the gravity of the injury.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has already been exhibited. Can I now call P488. That's the document we introduced at the beginning, at the beginning of this set of questions, concerning chemical weapons. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see paragraph 4. Again, in the first part, an opinion is expressed that with -- the use of these assets would be for the purpose of inflicting losses on enemy personnel. It says: "We believe that by destroying the columns of Muslim population from Stublic, Radava, and Brloska mountains, the Muslims could be forced to quickly surrender ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment. Sorry for that. The question of Mr. Tolimir was not recorded, not interpreted. Please repeat the question, not the text you have read into the record, but the question itself. We need it to understand the answer. Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 of this document, did General Tolimir express his opinion on the most advantageous way of destroying by using chemicals the pockets of strong resistance on their axis of attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is, in fact, item 5 which is now on the screen. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it must be a mistake in -- or in translation, because there is no item 5 in Serbian. That's why Mr. Tolimir was reading it as paragraph 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- passage 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think so. It's paragraph 2 of item 4. Thank you very much. It must be a mistake in the translation. Now you have heard the question, please answer this question, if possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From this, we clearly see that you are expressing your opinion on what should be done and what assets should be used. Now, allow me to express my opinion about your opinion. I think you were wrong here in suggesting the use of these assets and this conclusion is obvious from what I said about these assets and also the fact that I crushed the resistance in Brezova Ravna [Realtime transcript read in error "Brevo Ragna"] with cannons and not RPGs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, explain for the record, training assets were not sufficient. You had to use combat assets and other assets?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not use any chemicals because I knew their capability very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I've only asked to be heard for a second because at page 18, line 1, there's an indication of a location. It says "Brevo Ragna" and I'm not sure if that is accurate. Maybe it is, maybe it is not, but I would appreciate if that could be clarified for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, could you repeat what you said: "... also the fact that I crushed the resistance in," and please repeat this location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the sector of Brezova Ravan. Brezova Plain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I assume Mr. Gajic wanted to raise the same question. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at the last paragraph. It says: "We are of the opinion that we could force Muslims to surrender sooner if we would destroy groups -- if we destroyed groups of Muslim refugees fleeing in the direction of Stublici, Radava, and Brloska mountain." Were these locations on the axis of attack of the Rogatica Brigade or some other brigades?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The said features are completely on the other side of the front line, looking from Srebrenica. Brloska mountain is on the same axis, but I can't remember if there were any VRS forces on that axis on the attack. But even if there were, they scored absolutely no success. But for the information of the Trial Chamber, this whole terrain is very forbidding, wooded, almost impassable, and I remember it very well because that's where I was wounded in a confrontation with the Muslim forces from Zepa and Srebrenica in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: These locations Stublic, Radava and Brloska mountain, were they out of reach of your forces of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment and the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade? Was that the reason why it was suggested that some other forces which were on the axis of their attack should deal with them?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those locations are absolutely out of the range of our weapons, because we had only light infantry weapons, and, as far as I know, the Rogatica Brigade did not have any long-range weapons either that could be effective against this sector.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 65 ter 2001. That's the report of Mr. Butler, a Prosecution expert witness. After the cover page, we would need page 14 in English and page 16 in Serbian. Paragraph 2.14.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You saw the heading. He speaks of command responsibility and then in 2.14 he says, I'm quoting: "This sector -- this particular sector" -- starting again. 2.14: "In performing this mission, the sector was comprised of two administrations, the intelligence administration and the security administration." Please turn over the page in English. "Intelligence administration operated under the chief of intelligence operations and consisted of an intelligence centre (the 410th OBC), an associated analytical element, and the respective heads of the reconnaissance and Sabotage Units and radio reconnaissance unit. The security administration operated under the chief of security and consisted of a counter-intelligence group (KOG) and an associated analytical element. It also included the respective chief of the military police, and an officer responsible for ensuring the personal security of key officers of the Main Staff." Now bearing in mind what we saw in this text, could you tell us whether the organs of this sector and the administration, were they command or administration organs and explain to the Trial Chamber, if you can, the difference between command organs and administration organs.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security administration and the intelligence administration -- could you repeat the question, please. My thoughts went astray a little while I was listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber the difference between command and administration organs, and were the security and intelligence command or administration organs?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is that command relies upon clearly defined principles of unity of command and subordination and it is applied throughout the chain. It has an order-giving character and a clearly defined system of responsibility. In administration, in managing -- the very words administration and management are self-explanatory. They imply guidance and direction within the framework of the rules that govern certain areas. That means the security administration manages, advises, directs security organs which assets to use, which tactics to use, so it is quite logical that administration organs should be headed by the most experienced security officers who have gone in their career from the bottom to the top of the ladder and are able to provide good direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at this sentence in 2.14 where it says: "The security administration operated under the chief of intelligence operations" -- no, sorry. "The intelligence administration operated under the chief of intelligence operations." Was he able to administer this administration, the chief of intelligence, or was he doing something else? I will reformulate the question, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are talking very fast again, and you always should pause -- yes, but it doesn't help if you want to have it on the record. Otherwise, it's not said. So, please, the answer first. And then you may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to hear the answer of the witness first and then you may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting for the interpretation to be over. I was not thinking about your question. It says here that they operated under the command of the chief of intelligence. Actually, it was under the control of the chief of intelligence. I believe that here -- I would like to share an observation with you. I had an opportunity to read this expert report, and I don't think that it has resolved the role of staff officers in the staff. In my personal opinion, and in my view, the interpretation of that role was somewhat arbitrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you have just pointed out the key issue, and that is that the analysis do not take into account the staff role of the staff organs, can you tell us whether the staff role of the staff organ was to carry out decisions of the commander in the best possible way by consulting their subordinates as to how to carry out the commander's decision?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of the staff organs is to help the commander to resolve all the aspects of the problem and to propose how to use units which are within their authority. After such a proposal, the commander will make a decision that everybody has to carry out, from the very top to the very bottom. The commanders have exclusive right of command, and these are advisory organs that have their own authorities and competences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, you have just mentioned the advisory role of those organs. Yesterday you told us that the advisory role of the security and intelligence organs stops when the commander includes those organs into combat. Do they continue performing their advisory role, or is it the professional guidance of commanders who know better to carry out combat than the intelligence and security organs do?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment when a military police unit stops carrying out its normal security duties and starts carrying out combat duties, from that moment on, until the end of that combat mission, the security organ cannot have a guiding role, because those are no longer security tasks. Those are combat tasks that the commander deals with in keeping with the development of the combat situation at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In this paragraph, in line 5, there is the term "Heads of the reconnaissance and sabotage units and radio reconnaissance units." Do chiefs of security intelligence ever have command over those units, or is it the commanders of those units that have exclusive command of those units? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unit commanders have the command. Intelligence organs only propose the way how those units can be used in combat. And when I say "these units," I mean reconnaissance and sabotage units. The security organ proposed to the commander that, for example, a reconnaissance unit should be split into two or three reconnaissance groups. That's the proposal. The commander of a reconnaissance unit or the commander of a sabotage group, when he receives the order, he will carry out the order in keeping with his training and experience. He commands his unit, be it a group, a squad, or a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to say here who is it who give him his orders, his tasks? Is it the commander or the chief of security and intelligence? Is he on the strength of the command of the unit over which he has command or is he on the strength of the intelligence and security administration? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not very precise in that part of my answer. He receives his orders from the commander of the unit to which it is attached. If it is a sabotage unit, then it would be the corps commander. If is a reconnaissance unit, it can be the brigade commander or any other commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler doesn't understand one thing here. And that is, is the commander of a reconnaissance and sabotage unit part of the intelligence and security administration, or is he part of the unit over which he has command?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reconnaissance units are part of the organisation and establishment chain of tactical groups in higher levels of command. In our case, they were part of the operative compositions. They were part of the corps and the Main Staff. They were not on the strength of the intelligence administration. They were not part of the intelligence department. For example, like a brigade has battalions, infantry, motorised, and mechanised, it also has a reconnaissance unit as a combat unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this page of this report be admitted into evidence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we will hear the witness Butler in due course, and I would like to state he is not called as an expert witness by the Prosecution but as a -- but as a normal witness. This seems to be an expert report. Shall we perhaps postpone a decision about admission of this document? We don't know anything of the nature of this document. It will be perhaps used with Witness Butler in the next couple of days. What is your position? Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, this is on the list of exhibits to be used with Mr. Butler, who, I believe, is the next witness. Also, I don't see any harm in marking it for identification, at least until he -- until he testifies. But, otherwise, we don't have an objection to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, there's no concern about admission. It's only a question of practicability to have this part of the document admitted into evidence and later on, the whole document perhaps. That was my only concern. Would you agree with the proposal of Mr. Vanderpuye, to mark this part for identification, and we can then later on decide how to deal with the full report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to put more questions to the witness about the report, but I don't have the time. Mr. Butler has put forth his opinion. When he testifies, that will again be his opinion. And here we have a witness who was the commander of units, who was the chief of security administration. He is aware of all these things. He is familiar with all these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's no problem we admit this part, this page of the report into evidence, and it may be, later on, combined with the full report. This page will be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, pages 16 and 17 shall be admitted into evidence as Exhibit D291. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to call up D145. For the benefit of the witness, he spoke about this document during the examination-in-chief and he has already spoken about it during the cross-examination. I would kindly ask him to look at it again -- actually he spoke about the activities, not about the document itself. I have to say, for the record, that this is a document issued by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska by the sector for intelligence and security. It was sent on 24th of June, 1995, to the commander of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, who is now our witness and the commander of the 67th Communications Regiment. And this document, let's not read the whole of it, it refers to the Muslim attack and Sabotage Units from Zepa against the command post. Yesterday the witness spoke about that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, did you your command receive this document and was that the reason why you interrupted your sick-leave, in order to put up resistance against the enemy who had attacked the command post of the Main Staff? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that that was the first document that I received from the Main Staff when I returned from my sick-leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that this reconnaissance and sabotage unit left Zepa under the command of Ibrahim Mandzic and Avdo Palic and that it attacked the command post and captured a certain number of troops in the sector of Ruzina Voda and among them was Vladimir Mrdjan, who they kept in captivity until the moment the population was evacuated from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is true that attacks were carried out by the forces from both Srebrenica and Zepa. I remember a detail, something that happened after those events. We were in Borike in that villa, and you asked me how many people attacked us then in Crna Rijeka, and I said that there were several hundred troops. And then you showed me a document. It was a telegram, and I could see that there were 1200 men attacking us according to telegram. And then I joked and I told you, "General, you should have shown me on the day of the attack."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, did you receive intelligence to the effect that the Muslims in the Han Pijesak and Han Pogled sectors wanted to link up with the forces from Srebrenica and Zepa and forces from Tuzla and Kladanj? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to our intelligence, those were their intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's now look at the third paragraph in this document, where it says: "According to our information, the return of Naser Oric is connected with plans to commence combat operations from the Srebrenica enclave, which, supposedly, is conditioned by the possible taking of the Vis elevation in the Serbian municipality of Kalesija by the Muslim forces from the direction of Kalesija, whereby they would create conditions for further penetration towards the municipality of Sekovici. Following this, combat would supposedly begin from the direction of Kladanj towards the VRS defence lines in the zone of responsibility of the Vlasenica Brigade, when the units from Srebrenica would insert themselves towards Konjevic Polje via the sector of Buljim in the Milici municipality." My question is this: Do you know if Muslim forces carried out activities from the direction of Tuzla and Kalesija with an intention to take up the elevation of Vis in order to create conditions to link up the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, I believe that the Vis elevation was temporarily occupied by the Muslim forces at one point in time. Later on, in a conversation with Colonel Andric, who was still the commander of the brigade in Sekovici and whose birth place it was and he had -- participated personally in fighting around that elevation, I learnt about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D62. We see here a document -- can we zoom in so as to see better? I have to say for the record that it's a document from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 285th Eastern Bosnia Light Brigade, dated 28 June 1995. They plan and order combat operations. Let's look at this. Pursuant to the order of the deputy commander of the 28th Division, Major Ramiz Becirevic, number such and such, on measures to be taken, in terms of sabotage actions aimed at inflicting losses upon the aggressor on his troops and equipment, et cetera. "Upon receipt of the orders given me by brigade commanders Major Zulfo Tursunovic and Major Ibrahim Mandzic and by the assistant for intelligence in the division, Captain Ekrem Salihovic, I reviewed the overall situation with respect to this kind of ... action, and, based on earlier instructions, issued to the Chief of Staff, Major Ramo Cardakovic, by the chief of the General Staff, Brigadier General Enver Hadzihasanovic, I decided, together with Tursunovic and Mandzic, to proceed as follows: To form a number of sabotage groups of between a squad to reinforced platoon-strength, and dispatch them deep in the temporarily occupied territory for the purpose of inflicting on the aggressor maximum possible losses."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: If they formed these sabotage groups of squad to reinforced platoon-strength, how many men would that be per group in the then-Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One platoon is a military unit comprised of three squads, depending on the purpose of the unit. But, on average, it has 30 men. A reinforced platoon means it's reinforced with at least one squad or certain weapons for support or anti-armour weapons or other assets and it would have to have a minimum of 40 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Further down, he decides to do certain things. He says he formed nine sabotage groups. And then he enumerates the areas to which he has sent them. So he sent about 40 men to each of these sectors. And then he says: "All sabotage groups had the task to act simultaneously in two-hour intervals, in order to stretch enemy forces thin, to harass, confuse, create panic, and collect intelligence for the purpose of combat operations ... possibly going into action even before the start of the attack, if circumstances were favourable." My question is: Was it the case that in reality, in view of the strength of the resistance against the Main Staff, was it obvious that the Main Staff was being attacked by a number of groups from a number of directions at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The attack began in the morning of the 26th June when the 1st Sabotage Group, or groups, attacked the command post of the Main Staff, and while we were taking steps to repel the attack, when I was leading a tank company from the barracks in Han Pijesak, across the guard post and Pitoma Poljana, the company was ambushed. The captain of the company was wounded, as were several soldiers, and it was only armour and the protection of the tanks that saved them. Later on, perhaps two or three hours later, the company of APCs that arrived from Nova Kasaba or, rather, part of that company was also ambushed, but they managed to come out of it unscathed and repel the attack, so it was one first attack and then a synchronised attack, exactly as they had planned it. And allow me to add, because I know this terrain and this area very well and the features mentioned here, the first group had the task to attack the road, the Zljebovi Han Kram, and those were civilian targets. These are main roads. No army there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it is 10.30. We must have our first break now. We noted that the Prosecution exceeded the time they indicated for examination-in-chief. Now you are doing the same in your cross-examination. But, for planning purposes, it would be very helpful if you could give us an indication of the time you will use for the remainder of cross-examination after the break. Can I give us an indication?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since this is a 92 ter witness, I would have a lot more to ask him than the Prosecution did, even though they attached a large number of documents. But I will finish by the end of today, leaving enough time for the Prosecution to -- for their re-direct so that we can begin the next witness in due course, and I hope that I will finish within the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your first indication was four hours. Now you have used five hours. That's really a lot of time. I would like to invite you to shorten your cross-examination as much as possible. Mr. Vanderpuye, could you give us an indication about -- could you give us an indication about the time you will use for re-examination, as -- if can you say that at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At the moment, Mr. President, with the topics I -- I intend to broach on re-direct examination it looks to me that it will take me about an hour to do it. I don't know what other areas General Tolimir intends to go into on the cross-examination, but he has gone into a number of areas that I did not deal with in the direct examination and weren't dealt with in substance in the witness's prior testimony. So that's what I think now. It obviously depends, you know, on the nature of the answers that I get during the examination. But it appears, in any event, between us, that it is very unlikely at all that the next witness will start today. I will discuss it with my colleagues and Mr. Gajic, and perhaps we can come back to the Court with something more definite about the future scheduling of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it is not very realistic that we are able to start with the next witness today. He should be released for today. There is no need for him to wait. I would like to invite both parties how to make sure that this witness can be released today, because we have the next hearing only Wednesday next week, and it would be not very nice for the witness to stay here for such a long time. So that, please, make sure that you share the remaining time for today, for the remainder of the cross-examination and re-examination. We adjourn for the first break, and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Tolimir, I would like to ask the Defence to upload the two pages of D291, as a separate document, so that we can make a distinction between the full document and these two pages admitted into evidence. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With respect to that exhibit, actually, Your Honour, I had noticed in the transcript that you had indicated that Mr. Butler was not an expert and actually we have put him forth as such. So I don't know if that was maybe just something that was a mistake in the record, but that's what our position has been with respect to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification of your position. We will see how to proceed. Mr. Tolimir and the Prosecution, I hope you have a reached agreement about sharing the remaining time of today. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, once again. We haven't actually. I think we will try to do that. But to be fair, if General Tolimir needs to proceed beyond the amount of time that I've indicated that I require for re-direct examination, if -- and if the witness is able to stay, our position is it would not interfere substantially with the -- with the schedule of the next witness in any event. So if General Savcic is able to stay over until Wednesday, that's fine too, and then we can proceed accordingly. So I will leave it in the Chamber's hands to determine how best to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. For the scheduling purposes of the Prosecution, I have to say that our earlier estimate was made based on one and a half hours indicated by the Prosecution. However, since they extended this time, we had to increase our number of hours. I said that we are going to finish during this session and then the Prosecution can finish in the last session, in order for us to release the witness. Thank you. Can we now please look at the next page of this document. Thank you. Let's enlarge, and let's look at paragraph 1, which talks about losses. This is not good. This is something completely different. In paragraph 1 it says: "About 40 Chetniks were killed ..." But I don't see that on the screen and neither can the witness. There's some confusion here. We need the next page after this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, it was the previous page, page 1 -- last paragraph on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It reads: "About 40 Chetniks were killed and dozens were wounded. A significant quantity of infantry weapons were seized ..." And in line 4 it says that in the sector was -- there was a soldier from the 65th Communication Regiment wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, having in mind all these losses and such a large-scale attack, was that also an attempt to stretch our forces and to force the Main Staff to withdraw the troops from Sarajevo and feature of Vis, in order for them to achieve their designed operation of linking up? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is, in any event, a large-scale and coordinated action, precisely due to the fact that in mid-June there was a fiercest offensive launched against Sarajevo. The reinforced forces of the 1st Corps and even the 1st Corps of the 28th Division were participating, so the bulk of the forces were attacking the Trnovo axis. All the other operations carried out by the BH Army were intended to compel the command of the VRS to manoeuvre its troops and to prevent deeper penetrations into the territory along specific axes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that they attacked also a road where there were no military installations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document D816. 1D -- 1D816. Thank you. Can we please have it enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see that this is a document produced by Republika Srpska, Ministry of the Interior, public security department, sent on the 26th of June, which is exactly the day of the attack. It says: "Due in the incursion by a number of sabotage terrorist group in the Han Pijesak sector, immediately stop all traffic on the section of the road between Vlasenica-Han Pijesak-Sokolac, in both directions." Is this what you were referring to a minute ago in your answer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this document tendered into evidence. And we will need a new document after this one in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D816 shall be assigned Exhibit D292, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D52, please, in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting, I will say, for the record, that it was produced by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 2nd Corps Command, and that it is dated 8th of July, 1995. It contains information to be passed on -- actually, the results achieved by units and Land Forces. In order for me not to read the whole document, let's just look at paragraph 2. It says that: "60 Chetniks were liquidated and according to unconfirmed reports the aggressor suffered even greater losses and had many wounded. "In the village of Visnjica large quantities of ammunition were seized but the soldiers were exhausted and could not remove it, so the ammunition was destroyed, as were all the facilities that the aggressor could have used for military purposes." My question is: Was the number of casualties, because it says 60 Chetniks, and the destruction of entire villages forced the Main Staff to respond to these activities from demilitarised zones and to try to demilitarise them, in accordance with the agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have Prosecution 65 ter 05884. Thank you. 05241. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P2431. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It seems that I called up a different number by mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The -- Mr. Tolimir, you asked for 65 ter 5241; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order not to waste time, Mr. President, we can proceed with this document that we currently have on our screens. Can we just look at the next page. Thank you. Thank you. It seems that I have a wrong document again, and I finally realise that it is really a wrong document. Could we please have P1214. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here we see Directive number 7 issued by the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska, drafted on the 8th of March, 1995. During examination-in-chief, you were asked about the duties of General Tolimir with respect to reporting on combat readiness, and you said that I spoke about the enemy forces, et cetera. Now, we have a document here which was a directive for further operations, and we have main characteristics of the international military and political situation. Was that the role to be played by intelligence security organs to draft this item number 1 in any such directive? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you were on sick-leave when this directive was issued, you probably realised that, later on, this directive was something that referred to further operations. Are you aware that it was in force while you were on sick-leave and also after you came back?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during that time, when the -- this directive was issued and in the subsequent period, I wasn't familiar with the details of this directive. You can see that it was sent to the commands of operational units, whereas lower levels of commands did not need it so much for their day-to-day operations, because, practically, we were receiving daily or very specific assignments, depending on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We see that item number 1 speaks about the work of the Contact Group, and it says that: "The Contact Group has not really abandoned its plan for the former BH. However, it has reached an impasse and is now trying, through contacts with representatives of the RS, to find a cosmetic formula which would enable them to continue the process of a negotiation. America's latest initiatives are aimed at formally maintaining contact group unity and its own domination." Did this all reflect on the events in the battle-field among all the warring parties in the republic; and did you feel it specifically in your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, we did, not I personally as the commander of the unit, but each and every soldier felt it. And I can even add, every civilian. If I'm not going to waste too much time, let me just tell you this. In 1995, in the village of Tomina, on the west battle-field there was a Serbian village that was completely evacuated with the exception of one old woman. We asked her what she was doing there and she said all of this up to here is ours. So everybody was involved in this. Everybody was following the developments on the front, and everybody was expecting some solution to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that this old lady knew about some secret agreements that were still kept secret as to how far Republika Srpska would stretch and where the border with the Federation was going to be? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. She could not have known about any secret agreement. But, you know, rumours are rumours, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now you mentioned Sanski Most. Was that after you had received an order to travel to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't hear and understand where he was supposed to travel to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I left for Drvar on the 27th of July, and this could have happened sometime in mid-September. So after that, which was the time when some municipalities, such as Drvar, Petrovac and Kljuc, fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at paragraph 2 now, where it says: "By exerting pressure on the FRY and the RSK, the West has achieved the signing of agreement between the RSK and the NDH, the implementation of which creates favourable conditions for the RSK's economic reintegration into the NDH supported by a UN Security Council resolution, envisaging that Franjo Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic must approve any flow of goods from the FRY to the RSK or the RS ... this effort is aimed at ensuring the RSK's full economic reintegration into the NDH while making it dependant on it, and the Republika Srpska dependant on the Muslim government. This is the basic pre-condition for the political reintegration and recognition of Croatia and BH within their administrative borders." My question was: Now, after 15 years since peace was brokered, do we still have the same intentions in Republika Srpska that the Army of Republika Srpska was defending at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would object to the question, that it's vague. I don't know what particular principles General Tolimir is referring to, or objectives General Tolimir is referring to. If I could identify them, I think the witness can competently answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: After having quoted the lengthy part of the document, I am not in a position to fully understand your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will reformulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The second paragraph speaks of pressures on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbian Krajina that existed then. Do the pressures, both on the Federal Yugoslavia and Republika Srpska, continue today, to achieve America's aims in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say here something briefly, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If it could be brief, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you would like to consult -- you would like to consult Mr. Sladojevic? You would like to consult Mr. Sladojevic? You may do so. If it's possible to do it here in the courtroom, or shall we break? Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's not clear to me at this point that the purpose of the consultation relates to an issue that arises out of this witness' investigative capacity for the Karadzic Defence, in accordance with the terms that you defined for these purposes earlier in these proceedings. So if -- and I'm not inquiring as to the nature of a confidential communication, if there may be one, related to this witness's capacity as a Defence investigator, but it would be appreciated, and I think it would be required to state at least that it relates to such a purpose in order for such a consultation to occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would kindly ask Mr. Tolimir to consider if it is really necessary to put this question to the witness about America's -- that means the aims of the political -- the political aims of the United States of America today. If that relates in any way to this case. We could perhaps avoid bringing the witness under certain pressure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We're talking about the document, Directive number 7, that the Prosecution presented to a number of witnesses, and the Prosecution has asked this witness whether it was Tolimir's role to report during the briefing on that situation, and I said that, indeed, the first item in every directive, this is covered. Is it the role of the security and intelligence organs, I asked him, and he said yes. And I asked him whether these pressures on the Republika Srpska and Yugoslavia continue for the purpose of achieving the aims of the great powers in the Balkans. I just want to show how this type of information was topical then, as it is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How could an answer of the witness to this question help your Defence, discussing the aims of a state nowadays, 16 years later?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. He could assist by saying that the security and intelligence services got by information that is confirmed in practice, as it was confirmed in practice then. I'm not going to describe what America wants. Everybody knows that. But it is very pertinent to this case what America wanted during the war and why the cessation of hostilities signed in 1995 by the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina was extended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just so the Court is aware. We have no problem with the question. We agree with General Tolimir's general thrust, in terms of the relevance of the question. The objection is -- is, if you can call it that, was raised with respect to the request to consult with Mr. Sladojevic in the specific circumstances and that's the reason why I asked as to whether or not General Savcic can state for the record that the question involves his role as an investigator for the Karadzic Defence or certain privileges or confidences related to that as a pre-condition to the consultation itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I fully agree. That was my understanding as well. But I wanted to find a way to avoid any problem for the witness by rephrasing the question by Mr. Tolimir. Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I agree with what you have just said, Mr. Vanderpuye, regarding the fact that the issue really is -- with regard to the consultation between the witness and his legal advisor. I don't know whether the very consultation could be related to whether or not he should answer the question. So unless, since there will be no disclosure as to what the two will discuss, we might find a way out by allowing the witness to consult with his legal advisor on the way forward. There will be no disclosure of the matter what they are going to consult about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do understand the Court's concern and that is one that's -- that I share. It seems to me, however, that to the extent -- and General Savcic knows better than anybody. But to the extent that the question or the answer to the question may involve such a confidence, I think that it is important for him to say so, so that at least the Trial Chamber knows that this is the reason for the consultation; that is, I can't answer the question because I think it might involve my activities as a Defence investigator. But I think if he can't say that, then there is no basis for the consultation at all. And that is, in essence, the nature of my objection. We don't even have that basic predicate condition on the record for the consultation. And I'm not certain that Mr. Sladojevic represents General Savcic. I don't think that they have that relationship as attorney and client in these proceedings, and that I think is also important in terms of vetting this issue. I believe Mr. Sladojevic is President Karadzic's legal advisor which is a distinct position than being the legal advisor or the attorney for General Savcic. And this is exactly the situation where we may have a conflict between the interests of President Karadzic, as secured by Mr. Sladojevic, and the witness's obligations to respond to questions before the Trial Chamber, which are, essentially, within his own competence to protect or not protect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are perfectly correct that Mr. Sladojevic is not the legal advisor of Mr. Savcic. But I think we may overcome this problem if I ask Mr. Savcic: Do you see a conflict between your role as a witness in this case and your role as an investigator Mr. Karadzic's Defence team by asking -- by answering the question of Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that's precisely what I want to deal with through a brief consultation. If you had allowed it, it would have been resolved already. Because this is a directive to which the president of the republic as supreme commander is also associated. There's no reason for me not to answer the question. This directive was written at the time when I was at sick-leave. It was not sent to joint tactical units. I am familiar with it, to the extent that I have seen it before several times. I just wanted to consult Mr. Sladojevic briefly about this minor issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You may consult Mr. Sladojevic in our presence. You should switch off the microphones and consult him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just one word. The basis for these questions to the witness is that the document has been presented to the witness earlier at a previous trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Savcic, are you now able to answer the question of Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am, with a third proviso that this document was not known to me at the time when it originated. Instead, I was shown excerpts from it at an earlier trial. I can only repeat what I've said before. The role of intelligence and security organs is to make assessments of the military/political situation in the geo-strategic sense, the strategic and operative sense, and what is written here reflects precisely that activity of intelligence organs. As for the role of the great powers, I believe everybody knows about it, everybody views this role from their own point of view, and, of course, I have my own view which coincides with the view of General Tolimir. Everybody has their own view, and, of course -- at least I think it's pointless to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we turn two pages forward in this document, chapter 211, Muslim armed forces. Once we've read it I'll ask my question. That's page 3 in English. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Subheading: "Possible objective and plans of the Muslim forces." "After signing the agreement on a cease-fire and cessation of hostilities, not a segment of which are they respecting, the Muslims have embarked on the reorganisation of their armed forces ..." That's all I want to read from this. And in the last line of this paragraph, it says: "Should they fail, using NATO they would probably exert strong pressure on Republika Srpska to halt our counteroffensive. They will constantly threaten and possibly use NATO air force." Was there a constant threat of NATO air-strikes against the Army of Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska, and did these air-strikes eventually take place?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a threat of the use of NATO air force. And the air force of NATO was, indeed, used more than once for air-strikes against the forces and the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 4 on this page. I will quote: "The Muslims are planning to conduct the spring offensive on selected axes towards Sipovo, Srbobran, Vlasic, Teslic, Doboj, Brcko, Majevica, Kozluk, Sekovici, Vlasenica, Han Pijesak, Semizovac-Orlovo road, Trnovo, Borci, Nevesinje, Krupa" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down while reading names of locations. If you want to have it in the record, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Did Muslims indeed plan a spring offensive on these axes against Republika Srpska, and did you participate in deterring this offensive on several axes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the enumerated axes are axes where this spring offensive was carried out, indeed. I don't know only about what happened around Borci and Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at the following paragraph, and that paragraph starts with the words: "In the second stage ..." "In the second stage, they will probably keep up these activities in order to seize the rest of the RS territory and link up the Muslim-held territories in order to create a unitary state. They will focus on linking the enclaves and reaching the Drina River, continuing the attack along Jajce-Mrkonjic Grad-Kljuc-Sanski Most axis with the aim of joining up the forces of the 5th and the 7th Corps and seizing Borak and Nevesinje." My question is this: Towards the end of the offensive in which they participated from spring until the end of war, did they actually take Jajce and Mrkonjic Grad?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move onto the following page. We can now see information about the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia and their goal. I'm going to read just one passage. "Both the political and military leaderships of Croatia will exert political and military pressure on the Republic of Serbia and Krajina in order to reintegrate it into the independent Republic of Croatia. At the same time, in the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina" -- We can't see it here, I apologise. You don't see the part that I'm reading. Look at 2.2, "The Armed Forces of the Republic of Croatia," it is at the bottom of the page and you can't actually see the text. It is page 6 in English. Now you can see the text: "The Croatian political leadership will intensify military, economic and political pressure especially on the Republic of Serbian Krajina in order to reintegrate it into the independent Republic of Croatia." My question is this: Were these objectives achieved? As a result of the Croatian aggression against the Republic of Serbian Krajina, was the Republic of Serbian Krajina eventually reintegrated into the territory of the Republic of Croatia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
