utterances.text: Yes. The Croatian Army participated in the operations in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's move onto the following page to illustrate what you have just told us, in view of the fact that you were engaged on the axis of that attack that involved the forces of the Republic of Croatia. Thank you. We can now see the last paragraph on page 7 in English and the text that we have just seen in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last paragraph? Now the e-court has scrolled up and the text has gone missing from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Along the Grahovo and Glamoc lines the HV has deployed about 5.000 troops with the possibility of reinforcements. Further operations will follow if they assess that the" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this doesn't work. Please, indicate which paragraph you are reading from and then slow down while reading. It is not possible to follow. And most of that will be missing from the transcript. That is not your interest.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the interpretation will start working now when I start reading. "Along the Grahovo Glamoc lines, the HV has" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where are you reading from? Where are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an arrow pointing at the part of the English text in the last paragraph next to the paragraph that I'm reading from in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the last paragraph above number 3. It is not only necessary to have it on screen but we need an indication in the transcript. This is the reason why I asked for that. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. "Along the Grahovo and Glamoc lines, the HV has deployed around 5.000 troops with the possibility of reinforcements. Further operations will follow if they assess that a peaceful reintegration of the RSK into the NDH is not feasible with the ultimate goal of putting the Knin Krajina at an operative disadvantage by cutting it off."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question: This part of the assessment provided by the Main Staff of the Supreme Command was it implemented and did the Croatian army ultimately occupy part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, thus denying the contents of the agreement on the peaceful reintegration that had been signed prior to that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the Grahovo and Glamoc axis, from July 1995, the forces of two guards brigades of the Croatian Army were engaged. On the Grahovo axis there was the 4th Grahovo Brigade, I engaged with them on several occasions, and its second echelon is the Home Guard Regiment from Sinj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you participated in those operations and you were the chief of the security administration, tell us, is the task of the chief of security administration to prepare intelligence and submit to the commander to help him draft his combat documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When it comes to the intelligence and security organs, does that complete their part of the mission? When they submit intelligence on the enemy, do they continue to participate in the commander's decision on the further engagement of the troops? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This brings their main task to an end. They inform the commander about the political and military situation about the enemy and the -- the other assistants then proposed the use of the troops. And when I say that, I primarily mean the operative in our army, in the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call 65 ter 07425. It's the Prosecutor's document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see it now. This is a document issued by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, dated 10th July 1995. The title is: "Withdrawal of parts of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment forces from the area of Trnovo and sending them to the 2nd Krajina Corps area of responsibility." Order. The first item of the order reads: "During the night between July 31st and August 1, 1995, the 65th ZMTP forces are to be withdrawn from the present zone of utilisation, and upon finished preparations, the forces are to be sent to the Drvar where they will report to the regiment commander Major Malinic. Zoran is responsible for preparations and bringing part of the 65th ZMTP to the sector of Drvar." My question: Did you go to the command post in Drvar in keeping with this order? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait with your question. Now you put the question because it is not -- everything recorded what you have read into the record. Now your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For the record, I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Pursuant to the document that we have just read out from, and this is an order, were you dispatched to the command post in Drvar? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of July, even before this order was issued, on the day when Grahovo and Glamoc fell, I received an order from the commander of the Main Staff to urgently go to Drvar, together with my small combat unit, the size of a platoon, that had been engaged around Zepa. It took a few days to resolve the situation in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in order to withdraw most of the forces of the Protection Regiment from the area and for them to be sent to follow me a few days later and leave for Drvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the territory of Drvar, there was an offensive -- a joint offensive by Muslim and Croatian forces going on. Did you see anybody else in that theatre of war, or did you learn from any of the documents that any other officers were deployed in that theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the -- in the ensuing period, which was the month of August, dramatic things happened at the beginning of August in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It capitulated. It fell completely. As far as I can remember, almost the entire Main Staff, save for the chief of operations, was in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps at the command post in Ostrelj. That was the forward command post. As far as I can remember I saw almost all member of the Main Staff there. I went there very rarely, but I saw them all, and I remember one occasion when I saw you at Ostrelj as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know from combat documents that I was in Sanski Most and in Mrkonjic and so on and so forth during combat and that was when you had already been replaced by some other units? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did not have the good fortune to follow the work principle of other units. I was not relieved after a certain while. I stayed in the area until the 20th of October, until the moment a final cease-fire was agreed. I was in Banja Luka until the end of that year. I had several occasions to see you in the Sanski Most sector in the village of Tomina. I had been given a task to take a tank company to attack and then the bridge on the Sana had been blown up. I saw you there. There was a state of chaos. The troops were intermingled with the civilians. The situation was very difficult and it was very difficult to contain or control that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise having thought that you were relieved. I had in mind other units that were relieved and replaced in those sectors. Were you in those sectors during NATO air-strikes on the positions of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Army of the Republika Srpska? Do you know what facilities were destroyed during those air-strikes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present in the sector during NATO air-strikes on the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Actually, I heard about those air-strikes. And, as far as our forces are concerned, most of our communications centres were destroyed and the intention was to cut off all communication. And I saw the presence of drones that were above our heads all the time. They sent coordinates to the Croatian artillery, which pounded us for months, and that's how they forced us to abandon some of our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence? And in the meantime I will call up another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 7425 shall be assigned Exhibit D293. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up the Prosecutor 65 ter document 03986. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record this is Exhibit P2425. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is a document issued by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and it was sent on the 2nd of March, 1995, to the intelligence sections of the Drina Corps, the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, and the 67th Signals Regiment. There's an explanation here that the document was drafted by the Ministry of Interior and sent to the Main Staff. And the Main Staff sent it to the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know whether information was submitted to your command about the situation in Zepa and about the activities in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All topical information was submitted, if they concerned the situation in Zepa. The Motorised Battalion of the Protection Regiment was tasked with securing the axes leading from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the second paragraph in this document. Thank you. Where it says -- actually it is the refugee from Zepa who says: "At the beginning of January this year, a reorganisation of the Muslim armed forces in the area of Zepa was carried out when the so-called Light Vites Zepa [as interpreted] Brigade was established. After the mobilisation which was carried out recently, this unit numbers 1.220 conscripts." My question is this: Were aware of this before you had to return from sick-leave and participate in the defence against the attack that that brigade carried out against the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see the date. During my hospitalisation, I was not close to that area, and I did not receive any combat documents. However, I communicated over the telephone with everybody and I was aware of the most important things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Perhaps it was a misunderstanding. While the attack was being repelled in Zepa, were you kept informed by your deputies and assistants -- assistants?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says the staff was located --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We do not have the reference in the text. We cannot find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 2 in English. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not interpret the passage because it was not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please always give first the reference in B/C/S and in English, and then you may start reading after it has appeared on the screen. The interpreters need that. Please, again, page 2 in English. And which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second paragraph on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now the third paragraph: "Also located in the same building are the president of the municipality of Zepa, the president of the executive board, Hamdija Torlak, the general court, and the War Tribunal, whose president is Edem Omerovic from Zepa." My question is: Is it the case that in Zepa in the building of the agricultural complex there were headquarters of both the police and also the command and the Crisis Staff and other elements, such as the War Tribunal and the president of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where they were based, but I know they existed in the area of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This refugee from Zepa says in the last paragraph that in the -- last paragraph in Serbian, that's paragraph 3 in English. It says the civilian police is also based in the same building. Their chief is Hurem Sahic, and so on and so forth. My question is: Do you know if there were several such buildings in Zepa or there was just that one building of the agricultural complex that served as a basis for all sorts of armed forces, the police, and the command of the army, as this source indicates?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In international media, Zepa was portrayed as a small town with a population of several thousand, perhaps up to 20.000. However, Zepa is in fact a very small village of a dozen houses, and this agricultural complex, or perhaps it was a part of a factory, was the only such building, so they had nowhere else to use as headquarters for everything, the leadership of the municipality, the civilian police, and probably part of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 3 of this note in Serbian, and then we'll find a reference in English. That's the last, eighth, paragraph on page 3. It begins with the words: "The decision of the command of the Zepa Brigade ..." We have to go to the next page in English. I will quote from the Serbian: "The decision of the command of the Zepa Brigade in the event of an offensive against Zepa is to not allow the pullout of UNPROFOR from the enclave without the women and children. The source estimates that in the event of an attack by the VRS, the Zepa locals would put up resistance while the soldiers or military conscripts holding the status of refugees would pull out towards the Drina River, into improvised shelters" -- The rest is illegible. We'll wait while this appears in English on the screen. That's page 6, paragraph 1 in English. I cannot determine this in advance, because I don't have an English copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Since this note was submitted on the 2nd of March, 1993, and there is a reference to the decision of the command of the Zepa Brigade to pull out the women and children together with UNPROFOR while the -- the men would put up resistance, did it, indeed, happen, in practice?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the decision on the pullout of women and children from Zepa made back in March, when this man made the statement to the organs of the state security who, in their turn, made it available to the army?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when the decision was made, but it's obvious that that's what they did in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we see from this note that this Prebeg [phoen] knew about such a decision made by the command of the Zepa Brigade, this source knew it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see from the note that the source provided this information in March. It doesn't mean the decision was made in March. It could have been made earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday during examination-in-chief you said that you were in Sarajevo on the 4th of June. Tell us if you were in the Sarajevo Corps at the beginning of the war, and what can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was discussed the other time I testified, not here. Before the war, I served in Pancevo, and from there, I moved to Sarajevo, to teach in the military school in Sarajevo at the chair for special operations. That's where I was when the war broke out, and I left Sarajevo, together with the last units of the Yugoslav army, on the 6th of June, 1992, a couple of days of the well-known events at Zlovrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the attack against the military column of the JNA that was withdrawing from Sarajevo, in keeping with the decision of the then-federal secretary for national defence? That was 3rd May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, in the public and elsewhere, the fact is often neglected that most of the troops got killed on the 2nd of May, when most of the units from the Protection Regiment moved to intervene into the army hall. Almost all the officers of the sabotage detachment were killed then, headed by Marko Dadudovic [phoen] and other officers, Ivica Cvetkovic, Mr. Kastrati and a large number of soldiers. The shooting on the 2nd and 3rd of May could be heard in the barracks called Marshal Tito because that's in the centre, and I learned most of this after leaving the barracks Marsal Tito, when I became commander of the Protection Regiment, because among the officers of that regiment who were born in Bosnia and Herzegovina, most of them of suffered in this incident.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see D234. Page 31. Thank you. Page 31. This is 32. In e-court, it's 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see the heading: "Attack on the military column made up of JNA members in Dobrovoljacka Street, Sarajevo, on the 3rd of May, 1992." My question is: Is this the attack we were discussing, on the 3rd of May, when members of the sabotage detachment were killed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those members of the sabotage detachment got killed on the 2nd of May, the day before. What happened on the 3rd of May was the attack on the command of the 2nd Army District that was pulling in an agreement with the Bosnian leadership. They were leaving the peacetime location of the army command, and they were moving to another location.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just tell us how many people, how many men and how many were captured in that attack? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid to get the number wrong, but I have all the names of the men who were killed from my investigations, and I took over command of the Protection Regiment on the 6th of June. Many of the survivors who were natives of Bosnia and Herzegovina remained in service. I believe on the 2nd of May, some 15 men were killed, and it was mostly officers and young soldiers doing their compulsory military service. The monstrous part is this, that it was their colleagues, their fellow servicemen who had left the regiment just the day before, who killed them, and they were still wearing the same uniforms with the same insignia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see page 33 in the Serbian. That's 32 in e-court. Paragraph 3 from the bottom. And paragraph 2 from the bottom. That's the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "During the attack on the moving column, 23 were killed, 47 wounded, and 170 officers, junior officers, soldiers, and civilians in service were taken prisoner." Does this number, or do these numbers include the 15 men from the sabotage detachment you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a reference to those killed in the column on the 3rd of May. This does not include the members of the sabotage detachment who were killed the day before, the 2nd of May, at Skenderija. I believe there is no one involved in this job who has not seen the harrowing pictures of the streetcar in Skenderija. The soldiers were in two Pinzgauers and two ambulances. There were two ambulances because there were so many wounded and those two ambulances were set on fire. This is amply documented.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see page 35 in the Serbian. That's 34 in e-court. And we can see the list of the soldiers who were killed. The list of fallen officers and soldiers in the attack on the column. But if we look at the next -- next page, there's a total of 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness to see if he can find the names of those 15 men from the sabotage detachment in this list.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't really seen the first page, but I believe I saw the name of the commander Marko Labudovic but I did not see the name of platoon commanders, so I'm not sure if they are all on this list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the list from 1 to 12 be displayed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Those are the men. 6, 7, 8, 9 got killed on the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see the entire list of those killed, both from the sabotage detachment and the entire column. Look also at the list of active servicemen who were taken prisoner from the Sarajevo JNA hall, captured on the 2nd of May; and from the column, captured on the 3rd of May. Take your time and tell us when we can move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can move now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we can see those names. Can we move onto the following page, please. Thank you. I would like to thank the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Having seen the list, would you say that it contains all those who were killed in the column? And does it also contain the names of all those who were captured on those two days?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the killed are concerned, I believe that the list is complete. But I know that the number of captured was much higher. There are some other categories here, wounded, those who went missing. There were also many more wounded than are listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. There were about 170 soldiers captured, as it says on page 1, that we saw at the beginning, 23 -- 23 were killed, 47 were wounded, and about 170 were captured. That's what is -- has been recorded on page 33.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: You were in Sarajevo. You had information available to you. Can you make an inference as to why the column was attacked? Was it done on purpose in order to create an incident that would lead to a crisis in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I often ask myself that, not only when it comes to Sarajevo but also when it comes to Tuzla. It doesn't make sense to attack the enemy. At that time I thought that we were just opponents but we were already enemies. So there's no point in attacking your opponent when he's withdrawing. It should have been a -- perceived as a good development, a relief. There shouldn't have been any casualties. On the Muslim side there were no casualties. Only JNA members were hurt, and there were members of all peoples and ethnic groups there. I have just seen the name of Colonel Enes Taso. I knew him well. He was the commander of the 51st Mechanised Brigade in Pancevo before coming to Sarajevo. He was a Muslim. He just carried out his duty. He had been appointed to that position. He defended his state, as per the oath that he taken. I'm not clear on the motive. The only thing I see here is the wish to inflict losses and to compound the situation so much that it becomes uncontrollable, and beyond control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you said that on the 4th of June, at the beginning of war, a column was stopped in Zepa. Over 50 were captured and over 54 were killed. Do you think that the explanation is the same? Zepa, as you say, was small, and was it in a position to attack the VRS after it had been agreed that the VRS would take humanitarian aid to the units that were on Zlovrh? Was this a staged situation, intended to lead up to a crisis that would enable any further friendship impossible?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still think that that area up to the river Drina, including Zepa and all the other villages, Zepa is a common term for the entire area, I think that there should not have been any bullet fire there. But it was out of our hands, we suffered for as long as we could. But once the camel's back is broken, there is no going back. Especially when we had a lot of killed and wounded. There's no substitute for lost human lives. We didn't have a choice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to tender D234, in view of the fact that other witnesses have already testified in respect of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is already an exhibit but marked for identification, pending translation. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for having coming here and for having testified here. I apologise for all the questions that I had to put to you. This is my role. Thank you for everything. I wish you a long and happy life. I wish you a lot of health. I wish you a safe journey back home. May God be with you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This brings my cross-examination to an end. I -- I am leaving time for the Prosecutor, because I don't want the witness to have to stay in The Hague over the weekend. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But it's not clear if three quarters of an hour will be enough for re-examination by the Prosecution. Before we break, I would like to raise one matter, Mr. Vanderpuye, in relation to the next witness. I was astonished to hear that you will call him as an expert witness. We have no indication that you intend to call him as an expert witness. You have not included his reports in any of the notices of disclosure concerning expert witness reports, neither on the 13th of March, 2009, 26th of November, 2009, or the 29th of June, 2010. That should be clarified, but now we have to break. No further discussion on that, please. We adjourn and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Gajic and Mr. Vanderpuye on his feet. Perhaps, first, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, two pages from Mr. Butler's report, which is 65 ter 2001, those two pages have been uploaded under 65 ter 1D913. The two pages have been admitted as D291. Can this issue be resolved also in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, we have already decided to receive these two pages as an exhibit, D291. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First, I would like to know your position about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The expert issue, I take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- the expert issue of Mr. Butler. Because the Defence must have the opportunity to know your position. The Chamber would like to know it. Can you give us some information, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I can. Mr. President, I believe that the decision -- rather, the motions that you've cited referred to in general the expert witnesses that the Prosecution did not intend to call, either were going to call under 92 ter, or 92 bis, but aside from that, Mr. Butler is indicated in the Prosecution witness list as an OTP expert, which was appended to our filing. I believe that the Defence is on notice of this, particularly to the extent, as we can see, from the transcript during the cross-examination that General Tolimir himself referred to Mr. Butler as an expert. You are correct, though, I don't believe that there was a -- a specific or dedicated, I would say, 94 bis filing in relation to that. Nevertheless, I think that the provisions of 94 bis have been fully satisfied for two reasons. First, it is a notice requirement which -- though the practice is to give that notice pursuant to a filing, fundamentally, it a question of notice which the accused has been apprised of. Our filing of the witness list was on 13 April 2010, and, in fact, he was referred to as an expert in that witness list. He was also referred to as an expert during the opening statement, and, in fact, the accused himself referred to him as an expert. So I think the notice provisions of 94 bis are fully preserved. Also, he is present here -- well, before I get to that. His reports have all been disclosed to the accused. He has had them, for, I think, probably a number of years now. And the expert -- I see that we disclosed those reports in March of 2008, and the expert is, of course, available and present here to be fully cross-examined. I know that perhaps the Court was expecting a formal -- or looking for at least a formal 94 bis filing. I don't believe that there is one. I haven't had that opportunity to fully check that. But I am quite certain that the Defence is on notice. I don't believe they have an issue with respect to challenging his report or challenging his testimony on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you in a position to respond? What is your position on the role of Mr. Butler's role as a witness or expert witness? Or if not at the moment, you can leave it for a later stage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that he is an investigator who works for the OTP and is instructed by the Office of the Prosecutor, in terms of the method of work and the materials that be used. However, I don't have a problem with the OTP giving him whatever status they want to give him, and I propose that we should proceed with the witness who is in the courtroom here, today, in order to save him having to stay over for the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This is sufficient for the moment. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could have P1214 in e-court, please. And I think we'll have to go to page 2 in the English, just to keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, this is a document that was shown to you just a few minutes ago in cross-examination. You can see this is a directive for further operations, operation number 7. Now, you were directed to certain provisions of this document by General Tolimir, in particular some information contained in this document concerning the situation on the ground. Now you've been involved in security matters yourself. Is it fair to say that someone who is involved in providing information concerning this document, particularly security support for an operation, should be familiar with the full scope of the operation?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is not exactly very clear. The intelligence activity is an ongoing activity, and it is not carried out only before an operation. It goes on all the time. The intelligence collected is constantly analysed. In a specific case, when something is planned, be it an operation or a combat, then the collected intelligence is included in the accompanying combat documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this particular case we're talking about a directive for operations; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, if we are talking about a specific document, I repeat, that at the time, I was not abreast of the document. However, I can speak in theoretical terms. Based on my general military education and knowledge, I can say this is an assessment of the military and political situation, which encompassed a global assessment and the influence of the global political centres of power, and then the second part speaks about specific intelligence, the deployment of the enemy forces, and the methods and axes on which the territories of the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina were threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we go to page 7 of this document. I am afraid I don't have the B/C/S reference for it, but we'll find it soon enough. It's item number 3, and it relates to tasks of the Republika Srpska army. Do you see that heading?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we go to page 10, and it will be page 15 in the B/C/S, we should see the tasks that are assigned to the Drina Corps at the bottom of the page in the English and in the middle of the page in the B/C/S. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina Corps and then, tasks; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the second sentence of this provision it states that: "As many enemy forces as possible should be tied down by the diversionary and active combat operations on the north-west part of the front using operational and tactical camouflage measures, while in the direction of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible, preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves. By well planned and well -- by planned and well-thought out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Have you seen that before, General?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I saw this document was during my previous testimony. This is the second time I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in providing security support for such an operation, it would be fair to say that one would have to be familiar with the operation; right? Or such a task, as it's referred to.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood your question correctly, was your question that if somebody who is involved in security support should have been familiar with the operation? Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Somebody involved, yes, in providing security support for the generation of this particular directive should be familiar with the terms of the directive. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every member of the command has its -- his scope of activities, as I've already told you. The task of the security and intelligence sector is to provide intelligence and information about the enemy's intention. If we are talking about the strategic level. At the operative level, what matters is the deployment. At the tactical level, we go even deeper into the detail. And when that sector provides all that information, a member of the command, who is an operative, is in charge of further planning, especially the planning of those tasks will -- which will be proposed to the commander as the future tasks for the army units. In other words, every organ of the command has his scope of activities for which he is responsible. It is only logical that assistant commanders should have an idea of the whole plan. However, they don't have to have that idea. I'm giving you just some theoretical presumptions because I've seen this document only twice. I did not participate in its drafting or in its implementation at lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me take you to page number 14 in the English. Page 21 in the B/C/S. And we'll have to go to -- and by the way this is under item number 6, which says: "Support for combat operations."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We'll have to go to the third from the bottom paragraph in the English and the second paragraph from the top, I think, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What it says is that: "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall, through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependant on our goodwill, while, at the same time, avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." Have you seen this provision before?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I have to repeat that --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to know if you've seen --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I'm not familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- it because we don't have much time. Unless you want to come back on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not received interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to know if you've seen it without an explanation, unless you are free to come back on Wednesday, because I've only got 25 minutes left in the session. But you can proceed how you wish.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't like the tone. It sounds threatening. I don't remember having seen this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, I don't mean to press you, but if you're free to come back on Wednesday, then we can proceed at any length you wish. It's just that if we want to accommodate you and you will have to leave today, then I'm afraid I'm going to have to limit you to answer the questions as I put to them to you as precisely as possible. That's all. There is no threat involved here. It is just a question of expediting the proceedings. But, as I say, the decision is yours. You said it was only logical that a person involved in preparing the security support for a combat operation should have knowledge of the whole. In this case, you can see this provision, it would make sense, wouldn't it, that a person involved in drafting this document should have knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are on the last page of the document, it seems to me. I don't see that element, security support of combat. Where is that? Where is this thing that you have just read out? But, in principle, and pursuant to rule -- to the rules somebody who participated in the drafting of a document should have an idea of the whole that the document represents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to say that in the first answer, the witness said that he can be but doesn't necessarily have to be familiar with the whole. I think that the witness's words have to be interpreted correctly and not distorted when quoted back to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I know that wasn't directed at me, General, I'll just take that to be a legal objection to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In fact, it was directed to you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I respond to it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You could if you -- I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you wish me to respond to it, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You may, but if you put a further -- a previous answer of the witness to the witness again, you should be very precise. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me move on. Yesterday at transcript page 11, line 1 through 20, General Tolimir asked you some questions about Colonel Palic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And while you were talking about what you spoke to Colonel Palic about, you mentioned, and this is the last part of that exchange: "I can say here with full responsibility that even" -- I'm sorry, "that if they hadn't attacked us, if they had not launched offensives against us, the VRS would have never attacked that area because we did not either -- we did not either tactical operative or strategic reasons to place that area under our control." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This was in the context of the location of the IKM close to the lines. I mean, I'm sorry, the command post. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of strategic interest in that location, did that extend to the areas of the enclaves, Zepa and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke more about Zepa. I didn't mention Srebrenica at all. However, I put all that in a context of VRS's intentions for that area. That was the context where I put all that. I also explained, using the map where Muslim villages were, where Serbian villages were, and where the troops were employed [as interpreted]. In 1991 after the sixth attack by the Muslim forces, we responded to their attacks after having suffered huge losses. This is the context in which I spoke about things yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let show you 65 ter 2220, please. What we have here, rather, is a Drina Corps document. It's from the Command of the Drina Corps and is directed to the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade. And it says: "Pursuant to directive of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska," and it gives a strictly confidential number, "dated 19 November 1992, and an assessment of the situation, I have a decided ..." This document was signed by the commander of the corps, General Milenko Zivanovic. And it states under item 1: "Launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." And then it says: "Liberate and render useable the Milici-Konjevic Polje-Zvornik road and open a corridor towards Eastern Herzegovina." First of all, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you can see here a direct reference to "forcing the Muslim local population" out of those areas. Are you saying that that had no strategic value or was of no strategic interest?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you how things were. I can't remember the date, but somewhere at the beginning of November 1992, the Drina Corps was established. I would call this document empty words or empty threats. I remember that with my unit I carried out the first task in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps in the sector of Zvornik or, rather, the municipality of Zvornik, in the sector of Snagovo, Glodjansko Brdo, after major slaughter by the Muslim forces. General Zivanovic writes this, but his command did not even exist at the time. And as for the objectives, you can interpret them any way you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Actually, General, I was asking you to interpret them in the context of what you said during cross-examination when you said that the area had no strategic interest, or there was no strategic interest in the area.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that, I did not have in mind the army. I had in mind my unit who played a role in providing security for one part of the territory and the command post of the Main Staff. That's what I had in mind. However, in principle, being familiar with the overall situation, there's no single example that the Serb forces attacked first, in order to expel or transfer, I don't know what it says here. I don't know how individual commanders and officers worded that in their documents. It's really their problem. I can't interpret their words for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you 65 ter 24 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I would, actually, I didn't realise it wasn't a -- Mr. President, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask, Mr. Savcic, you just said on page 76, line 2 and 3: "General Zivanovic writes this, but his command did not even exist at that time." Are you saying that there was no Drina Corps Command at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what I'm trying to say. I said the corps was established sometime in early November, I believe. I can't remember the exact date. So it was not fully functional yet as an operative command. It was not a tight-knit, well-working team. Some organisation was still unfinished. Some units used to be in the Drina Corps, moved to the Eastern Bosnia Corps and vice versa. It is somehow too early for the corps command to plan a serious operation, because it hasn't gotten the -- the situation in their own area completely under control yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This is another explanation, but it existed at that time, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it did exist. You can see that from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2220 shall be assigned Exhibit P2434. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can -- we don't have it in e-court anymore. Okay. Let's move on to 65 ter 2494. And what you are going to see are the minutes of the Republika Srpska National Assembly, 53rd Session, from 28th August 1995. If we go to page 22 in the English and page 28 in the B/C/S, you will see that General Tolimir was present at that Assembly session. If we go to page 64 in the English and page 82 in the B/C/S, you'll see that President Karadzic was there at this 53rd Assembly Session. And if we go to page 68 in the English and page 87 in the B/C/S, we can see in the English, starting at the very last sentence of the paragraph, what President Karadzic says. The very last paragraph at the bottom of the page, last sentence begins and we'll go to the next page: "We absolutely cannot let ourselves get any ideas about them taking our traditional territories from us. To tell the truth --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please indicate the portion in the B/C/S that he is reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's about -- in the B/C/S it's in the bottom half of the page. If you can find the name Maksimovic, it's in the -- it's in the -- two sentences beyond that. I don't know if that assists the interpreters or the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't find it in the Serbian. I can't see Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just bear with me one moment, I'll find it for you. Should be in the second half of this paragraph that's been just blown up now.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was indicated by the cursor, where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to see it now?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you see where, beyond that, you'll see a reference to the locations of Drvar and Trebinje, following where it says "Maksimovic." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You will see, then, in the sentence that follows that, what I'm reading. And it says: "We absolutely cannot let ourselves get any ideas ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. "We absolutely cannot let ourselves get any ideas about them taking our traditional territories from us. To tell the truth, there are towns that we've grabbed for ourselves, and there were only 30 per cent of us. I can name as many of those as you want, but we cannot give up the towns where we made up 70 per cent." Continues: "Don't let this get around, but remember how many of us there were in Bratunac, how many in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how many in Rogatica, how many in Vlasenica, in Zvornik, et cetera. Due to strategic importance they had to become ours, and no one is practically questioning it anymore." That's what your now-boss said about this in 1995. I mean, can you tell us, do you stick to your testimony that these areas had no strategic interest?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I've said, and I repeat, once again, there was not a single case where I received orders to attack the Zepa enclave. It was an enclave beginning with May 1993. Not before, not after that. Unless I was attacked from that enclave, and when the lives of my soldiers, the territory, and the civilian population were threatened. I was not talking about the strategic objectives of the struggle of the Serbian people or the strategic decisions that were made everyone knows at what level, so I cannot debate other matters. I was talking exclusively about Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, you were asked some questions, as I mentioned before, about your encounter with Avdo Palic, and you talked about your conversation with him. Do you remember that? That was at yesterday's transcript, page 11. It was lines 1 through 20. You mentioned that had completed your elementary school, moved to Belgrade, that you heard about him during the war, you didn't know each other, and you had this conversation in Zepa. Do you remember that? You have to answer so that it can be recorded in the record.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you were also asked about your conversation or contact with Avdo Palic at another time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 7440 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What about the previous document? 65 ter 2494, are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm tendering the section of the quite extensive -- of the sections that I referred to and I think I have to identify them so that the Registry can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine. Then it will be received as a separate document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Portions that were mentioned in this hearing from the 65 ter document 2494 shall be assigned Exhibit P2435. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks. I -- I was hoping to have 65 ter 7440. Not available. Okay. All right. I think we have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, General?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it's a statement that you gave on the 12th of July, 2006; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you remember giving the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we go to the next page. I think it should also be the next page in the B/C/S. Actually, I think it's the preceding page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You were -- you gave this statement, it says, and you were instructed that you were to tell the truth and not withhold any information. Do you remember that having been done?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the usual procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we go to page 4 in the English, and it should be the next-to-last page, I think, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We will see here that you were asked if you made contact with Palic, in what way, and what kind of conversation did you have. Do you see that in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the whole page is here. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me see if I can help you. The cursor actually is indicating it. Near where it says "25 July," you can see what follows that is that question.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in your answer, you said that you made contact with Palic in the sense that you introduced yourself, stating your rank, name, surname, and function in the VRS, and that he replied, asking about your wounds, referring to the time that you were injured in 1992. And you said here that he also tried to ask questions with regard to the status and treatment of the people wounded -- wounded persons, I'm sorry, and soldiers of the Zepa Brigade. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how the conversation went, approximately. Not the status but the evacuation. I told him I was not a negotiator, and I cannot in any way influence the treatment of anyone among the population of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you testified here yesterday, you said that you: "... took the opportunity and asked him, If it was not necessary, why did you attack us on 4th of July ... and then I gave him all the -- I gave him all the dates from the outset of the attacks. And I told him that we responded to every fifth or sixth of their attacks when we could no longer tolerate losses." You didn't mention that when you gave your statement in 2006, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did I not mention?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That part of the conversation that you recounted here for us yesterday that I just read.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, nobody in this interview here asked me about the details of my conversation with Avdo Palic. Instead, since there was a lengthy investigation into the fate of that man, I was asked about that. There was a completely different set of questions before the MUP of Republika Srpska and the investigators of the OTP. There was never an occasion where I failed to answer a question that was asked of me. I was not holding back or covering up anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And one more thing, if you allow me. Avdo Palic named his detachment 4th of June, in memory and celebration of the killing of Serbian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me take a little bit lower down the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, we have now two possibilities. One is to adjourn and continue the re-examination with the witness next Wednesday; or to conclude the re-examination now. We have to adjourn because another trial is using this courtroom and they need preparation for some protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand. What I'd like to do is what we've done before which is to hold him over and I will reconsider the matter, or fully consider the matter, apprise the Trial Chamber if there is a change in our position, and, if so, then we'll let him know, let Mr. Sladojevic know and the parties know, to discharge him. But if not, then to have him back here on Wednesday. With the Court's leave, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there is no other way to handle the situation. When will you be in a position to give notice if you need Mr. Savcic on Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I will hopefully be able to do it by the end of the day, as I've done before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, you have heard the position of Mr. Vanderpuye. It is not clear now if you have to stay until next Wednesday or if this concludes your examination-in-chief -- your examination in this trial. You will be informed as soon as possible about the situation. This is very unfortunate, but it was a very lengthy interrogation by both parties, which was not foreseen by us. Thank you very much. We have to adjourn, and we will -- the Chamber will resume next Wednesday, I don't know of -- in the morning or in the afternoon -- in the afternoon, 2.15, in Courtroom II, in this courtroom. Thank you very much. Next week, as indicated earlier, Judges Mindua and Nyambe will sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, 29th day of June, 2011, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
